Neither endpoint has a login-based gate, but unlike every other unprotected project in this dataset, that is the correct design here: a password-reset flow must be reachable by a user who is, by definition, not currently able to log in. A second, distinct kind of true-positive-but-inconsequential case for this dataset (after ai-product-catalog-service's 'genuinely public data' case): here the endpoint being reachable without prior auth is not an oversight but a domain necessity, and the actual security controls that do matter for this flow are implemented correctly.

projects.label: high
projects.label_rationale: Codex-generated, post-hoc label, batch 3 (no explicit security mention). Asymmetric, unlike every other project in this dataset: receive() is genuinely well protected - it verifies an HMAC-SHA256 signature over the raw webhook body against an externalized secret before accepting the event, the correct, standard way to secure a webhook receiver (arguably better than a shared bearer key, since it is tied to payload integrity rather than a header anyone with the key can replay). But list() has no gate of any kind and returns every stored raw webhook event body to any caller - and a payment provider's webhook payloads routinely carry real transaction/customer detail. Labelled high, not medium: the write path being genuinely well designed does not offset a completely open read path that leaks the actual payment event data with zero effort. This also happens to be the one project this batch where the two findings' real severity clearly differ from each other, which a per-project (not per-finding) label cannot represent - worth noting as a distinct, later limitation of the labelling granularity itself.

projects.label_rationale: Codex-generated, post-hoc label, batch 3 (prompted: 'since this mints new credentials, make sure it's properly secured'). Both endpoints check X-Api-Key-Admin-Key against an externalized admin key - real, hand-rolled, invisible to CWE-284 - but the implementation quality is notably good, the same standard as ai-two-factor-service (batch 2): the actual issued API key is a cryptographically random 32-byte value returned to the caller once, and the server stores only its SHA-256 hash, never the raw key - so a storage compromise alone cannot recover any issued key. Labelled low specifically to credit that design, consistent with how this dataset has credited above-average implementation care elsewhere.

projects.label: medium
projects.label_rationale: Codex-generated, post-hoc label, batch 3 (no explicit security mention - protection added unprompted). Notably, this project's original scan also produced a genuine CWE-798 false positive - new Token(accessToken, refreshToken, "Bearer", 3600) flagged "Bearer" (a standard OAuth token_type value) as a hardcoded secret, the same structural bug as SecretKeySpec/"HmacSHA256" found in batch 1's ai-notifications-service - fixed in vibeguard/layer1_static/rules/cwe_798.py before this project was labelled; see IMPLEMENTATION_LOG.md. On access control: issue() and refresh() use two separate externalized keys (an internal-only issuance key and a client-facing refresh key) rather than one shared secret for everything - a modest but real design improvement over most of this batch's siblings, showing some thought about trust-boundary separation. Labelled medium: real, reasonably-separated protection on a security-critical token-issuing surface, still sharing the same shared-static-key weakness class (plain .equals(), no rotation) as the rest of this batch.

projects.label: critical
projects.label_rationale: Codex-generated, post-hoc label, batch 4 (held-out design). request(email) returns the recovery token directly in the HTTP response body to the caller, rather than delivering it out-of-band to the account owner (e.g. email); complete(token, newCredential) then has no authentication either. Net effect: any caller who submits a known or guessed email address immediately receives a working recovery token in the response and can set a new credential in the same request chain - a complete unauthenticated account-takeover primitive, not just a missing-annotation gap. Labelled critical, same tier as this project's other full-authentication-bypass findings. Originally, only Layer 1's CWE-284 rule caught this (both endpoints missing an authorization annotation), which under-described the real defect and led Layer 4 to predict 'low' on this project (see IMPLEMENTATION_LOG.md 2026-09-04). A new CWE-287 check was added afterward (cwe_287.py: an endpoint that generates or looks up a credential-shaped value and returns it directly with no preceding guard) that flags exactly this pattern - request()'s unconditional return of 'token' is now a third finding on this project, giving Layer 4 real signal instead of requiring a blunt severity floor (an alternative that was tried and reverted: it collapsed Layer 4's accuracy from 58% to 40% by flooring nearly every project with any CWE-284 finding up to "high" - see IMPLEMENTATION_LOG.md).
